There has been a flurry of recent interest in *guessing*. Most of this work has taken for granted something like the following principle:

Guess the Most Probable
:    If one is asked _Q^?^_, and responds by guessing a complete answer, that answer is appropriate iff it is the most probable answer, given your credences, to the question.

Something like **Guess the Most Probable** is a consequence of views defended by Sophie @Horowitz2019,^[Horowitz only commits to this for cases where there are only two possible answers, but doesn't give any indication that the principle won't generalise further.] Kevin Dorst and Matthew Mandelkern [-@DorstMandlekern2022], Ben @Holguin2022, Matthias @Skipper2023, Richard @Teague2024, and Niels Linnemann and Feraz Azhar [-@LinnemannAzhar2025]. A puzzle that Helena @Fang2026 raises for a generalisation of **Guess the Most Probable** might make one suspect that there will be problem cases for it. The point of this note is to build on Fang's idea and describe three cases where **Guess the Most Probable** fails. In all cases, some guesses which are not the most probable are permitted, and indeed in all three the most probable guess seems defective in notable ways.^[This is not to say that it is impermissible; the cases are hard, and any answer might seem defective. But in all cases the most probable answer seems weird enough that it permits alternative answers.]

# Guess the Order

At the start of every Premier League season, the _Guardian Football Weekly_ asks each of its panelists to guess the order that the 20 teams will finish in. This is obviously absurd; there are 20! combinations, and while some can be ruled out fairly comprehensively, there are too many reasonable ones to guess any with any confidence. But guess they do, and it is a useful framing device for talking about the upcoming seasons.

Inspired by that, I started looking at guessing the order of finishers in somewhat smaller competitions. So consider a simple four team league, where each team plays each other once, not twice as in the Premier League. You're probably familiar with these competitions; they are the standard form of the group stage at major international tournaments. We have four teams, imaginatively called A, B, C and D, and our expert is asked to guess the order that they'll finish in.

Our expert has to deal with two kinds of uncertainty. 

First, she doesn't know exactly how good each team is. She knows each team has an underlying quality, and for each team she has a distribution over their possible quality values, but she could be wrong. We'll simplify greatly; in each case the probability distribution is a normal distribution with identifiable mean and variance. Cruciall, she is very unsure about one of the teams, in this case C. For C, the variance in her view about the quality is much higher than for the other teams.

Second, soccer games are just random. You may remember Saudi Arabia beating Argentina in the 2022 World Cup. That was not because Saudi Arabia was the better team; sometimes the better team loses. The closer the teams are in quality, the more likely an upset is. But even for quite large quality differences, like Saudi Arabia and Argentina, the upset is possible.

Here's how I modelled that.^[AI acknowledgment: I used Claude Opus 5.5 to build this model, having explained to it the kind of tournament that I wanted. Once it was done, it came up unprompted with some summary statistics about the model which in turn I use below.]

Each team $i$ has a real quality $q_i$. In each tournament simulation, the qualities are drawn from the normal distributions with means and standard deviations described in @tbl-quality. In any game, we start with the difference $d$ between the two team qualities (remember quality is held fixed across a tournament). If the home team^[`Home team' here is just the first listed team. We are not assuming any home field advantage.] is better, $d$ is positive; if they are worse $d$ is negative. Then we add a noise parameter drawn from $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and tripled. If the absolute value of that is less than 1.2, the game is a draw. Otherwise, if it's positive the home team wins, and if it's negative the away team wins. The value of 1.2 was picked to get a reasonable number of draws; otherwise it is arbitrary.

[Insert tbl-quality here]

To see what the probabilities were for various outcomes, we then simulated the season two million times. As in regular soccer, a team got three points for a win, and one point for a draw. After three games, we used a randomiser to split teams on equal points.^[We could have tried to simulate not just results but scores, then used tie-breaking procedures, but this was getting complicated enough.] And we measured how often each of the 24 possible permutations of the teams came up over those runs.

Now this model obviously leaves out a lot. It doesn't allow for team quality changing over time, due to injuries. It doesn't allow for teams matching up particularly well or badly against other teams. But it's complicated enough to serve as an illustration.

Assume our expert knows her own mind, so she knows the numbers in @tbl-quality. And she knows how team quality relates to win probabilities, via noise parameters. She has just as many computational resources as we do, so she can build all the tables you'll see here. And she is asked, just like the podcast panelists, to guess the order in which teams will finish in this group.

If she gives a complete answer, and really that's what panelists are supposed to do, and **Guess the Most Probable** is correct, then there is only one permissible answer. It's ACBD. The numbers are shown in @tbl-rank-frequency.

[Insert tbl-rank-frequency]

But that's a surprising guess for at least three reasons.

First, she thinks that B is probably better than C. The mean of B's quality distribution is higher than the mean of C's. It's completely reasonable to rank teams in a task like this by your mean estimate of their quality. (I suspect that's more or less what people really do when asked to produce these rankings.)

Second, there are some statistics where our expert will, probably, do better if she guesses ABCD than if she guesses ACBD. This is not really a coincidence given the first point. There are six pairs of teams in the tournament, and we can ask for each pair who finished higher in any tournament run. We can also ask whether the actual order of the teams matches the expert's prediction of their order. It turns out, as shown in @tbl-pair-match, that in expectation she matches more pairs by guessing ABCD than guessing ACBD.

Third, she might be interested in the four questions _Who will finish in place i?_ for $i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4}$. As @tbl-finishing-place shows, she will on average answer more of those questions correctly by guessing ABCD than by guessing ACBD.

The point of these last two considerations is not that they are extra questions over and above what the finishing order is. To guess ABCD is, inter alia, to guess that B will finish second, and that B will finish above C. All that we need to make ABCD a sensible guess is that guesser cares about these extra things that she commits herself to when she guesses an order.
